newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Punt fall exacerbates Irish currency dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Punt fall exacerbates Irish currency dilemma.

text.p: The Irish pound's drop to seven-year lows against sterling on Wednesday exacerbates the currency dilemma facing the Irish authorities, analysts said.

Despite growing concern that punt weakness against sterling could fuel inflation, Ireland's central bank cannot make any move to support the cross rate without driving the punt higher in the ERM and risking a breach of its 15 percent ceiling.
"There have very few policy options they can go for or that they would want to go for," said Eoin Fahy, economist at Ulster Bank.
Raising interest rates or intervening to support the punt against sterling risks driving it upward in the ERM where it is currently trading 12.6 percent above the weakest currency, the French franc.
"You cannot be 12.5 percent above the bottom of the band and raise interest rates. It just shows that you are treating the ERM with a distinct lack of enthusiasm if you do that," Fahy said.

Analysts say revaluation remains an option but many believe the government is reluctant to go down that road at present as it would leave the Irish economy exposed to a sharp drop in sterling at a later date.

"My own feeling is that the central bank would prefer the revaluation option but the Department of Finance dictates currency policy and I would imagine that they would still be cautious about going down the revaluation route," Pat O'Sullivan, economist at AIB Group Treasury, told Reuters.
Fahy says a revaluation at this point in time does not make sense.

"By revaluing the Irish pound, you are moving it up to follow sterling but you cannot move it back down again if, at a later stage, sterling falls and the vast majority of commentators think that sterling is going to fall."
"I think the only option is to batten down the hatches and hope this goes away and to struggle on, struggle on, struggle on until the very last possible minute before you take any action," he said.

But other analysts say the pressure on the Irish authorities to do something could grow if sterling continues its relentless rise against the mark, particularly if it manages to breach the 3.10 level.

"If sterling/mark goes up to 3.10 or 3.11, you should see mark/Irish pushing its ERM bands...In that scenario, we are very much closer to a revaluation than we were even last week," AIB's O'Sullivan said.
Some dealers believe, however, that the punt may not follow sterling much beyond its current levels of 2.70-2.71 against the mark.

"Even if you have a revaluation now, you won't necessarily see the Irish pound any higher than it is at the moment so I think the markets will be a bit wary of the Irish pound against the mark from here on," one noted.

If this happens, analysts say the central bank may well be prepared to sit tight and let the sterling/Irish rate take the strain despite the inflationary risks, hoping that the competitive pressures in the Irish economy offset the currency's weakness.
They note that the bank has done it before.

"The last big sterling rally was in the late 1980s when it peaked at over 3.25 marks. Irish authorities let the sterling/Irish rate fall to 81.5 pence and held the mark/Irish rate stable at 2.67 even though the Irish currency was devalued in 1986," AIB's bond unit said.
